newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: RUGBY UNION-IRISH SEEK TO BUILD ON ASHTON FACTOR.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-IRISH SEEK TO BUILD ON ASHTON FACTOR.

text.p: Ireland's coaching advisor Brian Ashton prepared to renew aquaintance with old friends this weekend denying his in-depth knowledge of England's players would prove decisive in Saturday's Five Nations encounter at Lansdowne Road.
"It is not an advantage, nor have I tried to make it into an advantage," said Ashton, who used to work alongside rival coach Jack Rowell and captain Phil de Glanville at English club champions Bath
"What you've got to do as a coach is work on your own team's game first. You then look at themes in the opposition's game before working on any of their weaknesses, if there are any," he added.
Ashton, who quit Bath in early January and was appointed Ireland coach inside four days following the resignation of New Zealander Murray Kidd, has already been responsible for lifting Irish morale.
Under Kidd, who was appointed as the country's first full-time coach in October 1995, Ireland lost six out of nine internationals, including a 37-29 defeat by Italy in the New Year.
Ashton had barely any input before the 32-15 home defeat by France last month, but helped guide his new team to a 26-25 win over Wales in Cardiff two weeks ago.
Now he has been presented with an instant chance to remind Rowell of his talents in a match both sides need to win to stay on course for a Triple Crown-winning season.
"We had a good working relationship for six or seven years at Bath but I suspect my approach was always more expansive than his (Rowell's) ever was," Ashton said.
"He was more committed to winning at all costs. But if you look at the results, the balance clearly worked."
Ireland's management team see England's pack as posing the biggest threat.
"England have an exceptionally strong pack as they showed at Twickenham when they destroyed us last year, and again this year in the second half against Scotland," said team manager Pat Whelan.

"But our pack has been pretty much the same all season and that has helped to build confidence amongst the forwards. They will go on to the pitch on Saturday united and knowing they can get the better of the English."
Whelan said Ireland had been boosted by news that both prop forward Nick Popplewell and flanker David Corkery, nursing a hamstring strain and a broken finger respectively, would play on Saturday.
Centre Jonathan Bell, who scored a try against Wales, has also recovered from a rib injury.
The Irish have made only one change to the side who beat the Welsh, James Topping coming in on the left wing in the place of Dominic Crotty.
England have meanwhile retained the side who scored a record 41-13 win over Scotland in their opening Five Nations match at Twickenham.

Rowell, bidding to lead England to a fourth Grand Slam in seven years, is wary of the challenge that lies ahead having seen Ireland score a crushing 17-3 home win in 1993 and win again at Twickenham the following year.
"Brian has excelled at club level and now has the chance at international level. He will have Ireland well organised and highly motivated for Saturday," said Rowell.
